subject.title: Before the Wind
subject.author: Kathleen Jamie
subject.text:
If Im to happen upon the hill
where cherries grow wild
it better be soon, or the yellow-
eyed birds will come squabbling

claiming the fruit for their own.
Wild means stones barely
clothed in flesh, but that's rich
coming from me. A mouth

contains a cherry, a cherry
a stone, a stone
the flowering branch
I must find before the wind

scatters all trace of its blossom,
and the fruit comes, and yellow-eyed birds.

title: Before She Picked the Fight, She Picked the Cherries
standfirst: In 2004 Kathleen Jamie published fourteen quiet lines about racing garden birds for wild cherries. Four years later she picked a public fight with an entire school of nature writing — and this poem already knew which side of it she'd be on.

sections.heading: A Race She Admits She'll Probably Lose
sections.body:
"If Im to happen upon the hill / where cherries grow wild" — the poem's very first move is a hedge. Not *I will*, but *if*, qualified again a line later by *it better be soon*: this is someone talking herself into a walk she isn't sure she can finish before the competition gets there. The competition is birds. Wild cherries, she reminds herself with a kind of clinical honesty, are mostly stone — "stones barely / clothed in flesh" — and then she catches the unfairness of judging any creature's flesh and turns the joke on her own: "but that's rich / coming from me."

There is no ridge in this poem, no vantage point from which a human watches nature do something impressive at a safe distance. She is down among the "yellow-eyed birds," after the same scant fruit, on their schedule rather than hers, and by her own account not obviously going to win. That is a particular kind of nature encounter: not observation from outside a scene, but competition inside one, with the odds stated plainly rather than smoothed over.

sections.heading: Fourteen Lines Built Like a Sonnet, With the Rhyme Taken Out
sections.body:
Count the lines and the shape gives itself away: three stanzas of four lines, then a closing couplet — the skeleton of an English sonnet, quatrain-quatrain-quatrain-couplet, with none of the metre or rhyme filled in. Nothing forces that architecture onto fourteen lines this short and this plain-spoken; Jamie built a form designed for argument and a turn, then argued in ordinary, unrhymed sentences instead.

The turn, when it comes, runs backward before it runs forward. "Coming from me. A mouth / contains a cherry, a cherry / a stone, a stone / the flowering branch I must find" nests each thing inside the last — mouth, cherry, stone, branch — walking from the eaten fruit back to the blossom it grew from, before the closing couplet sends time moving forward again: the wind "scatters all trace of its blossom, / and the fruit comes, and yellow-eyed birds" — the same birds the poem opened with, arriving exactly on cue.

Nicholas Allen, introducing the poem for [the Willson Center](https://willson.uga.edu/11068-2) at the University of Georgia, wrote that "'Before the Wind' begins as a poem of observation and ends as something else," and that "a short string of sentences like this can braid a world together." Jamie does something similar elsewhere in the same book, on a smaller scale — [a review of The Tree House](https://richardcarter.com/reviews/book-review-the-tree-house-by-kathleen-jamie/) singled out a poem built from a single kittiwake feather washed up on a beach, and how little studying one feather can tell you about the whole bird.

sections.heading: The Year She Changed the Subject
sections.body:
"Before the Wind" ran in the June 2004 issue of Poetry, in a themed survey of British verse that also carried [poems by Christopher Logue](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/issue/71406/june-2004) and Jo Shapcott, plus a run of Don Paterson's translations from Rilke. It landed the same year as Jamie's collection The Tree House, which won the Forward Prize for best collection and marked, by the account of [one 2005 interview](https://www.irishtimes.com/culture/a-citizen-of-the-natural-world-1.455889), a real change of direction: away from the Scottish identity and gender politics that had driven her two previous books, Queen of Sheba (1994) and Jizzen (1999) — the latter named for an old Scots word for childbirth — and toward the cherry-and-bird scale of attention this poem works at.

Jamie had been publishing a long time by then. She studied philosophy at the University of Edinburgh and brought out her first collection, Black Spiders, in 1982, the year she turned twenty. Looking back on that early start from the vantage of The Tree House, she was characteristically unsentimental about it: "If I had my time again, I wouldn't do it. I'd arrive on the scene at the age of about 33."

sections.heading: Four Years Later, She Picked a Fight With a Type of Man
sections.body:
By 2008, Jamie had turned this same instinct into an argument. Reviewing Robert Macfarlane's The Wild Places for the [London Review of Books](https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v30/n05/kathleen-jamie/a-lone-enraptured-male), she objected to a kind of nature writing built almost entirely around a single heroic witness — "We see him swimming, climbing, looking, feeling, hearing, responding" — in landscapes she pointed out were rarely as empty of other people as they read on the page: "For a long time, the wild land was a working place." Her title for the piece, delivered with open mockery, was "A Lone Enraptured Male"; her sharpest line asked, of the type of writer she meant, "What's that coming over the hill? A white, middle-class Englishman!"

"Before the Wind" was written before that argument existed as an argument, but it already refuses the shape Jamie would later object to. There is no summit here, no solitary figure claiming a landscape by describing it well. There is a woman losing a race to birds for fruit not much bigger than its own stone, admitting in the same breath that she has no high ground to argue from. The essay named the type four years later; the poem had already declined to be it.

sections.heading: What Stayed After the Tree House
sections.body:
The Tree House was well received on release — [one review](https://indiecateditorial.substack.com/p/the-tree-house-by-kathleen-jamie) called it "exquisitely crafted" and noted that, next to the sharper, more polemical Queen of Sheba a decade earlier, "not a word is wasted or extraneous." Jamie kept working the same seam afterward in prose: her essay collections Findings and Sightlines carried the close, unglamorous attention of a poem like this one into nonfiction, and Sightlines went on to win the John Burroughs Medal and the Orion Book Award in the United States.

In August 2021 she was appointed Scotland's Makar, the fourth poet to hold the post since the Scottish Parliament created it, serving until December 2024. It is a long way, in one sense, from a woman racing garden birds up a hill for wild cherries. In another sense it is not far at all: the same refusal to overstate the view, applied at national scale instead of at the scale of one afternoon and one tree.
